category: Attack rate: before vs after an intervention
stem: A summer camp ran two sessions of the same activity. Session 1, with no hand-washing rule, had a stomach-illness attack rate of 45 percent. Session 2, with a hand-washing rule added and nothing else changed, had an attack rate of 12 percent. The drop from 45 to 12 percent is best described as:

options.A: proof that the pathogen disappeared on its own
options.B: the measured effect of adding the hand-washing rule
options.C: evidence that Session 2 simply had more campers
options.D: a sign that the attack rate is not a useful number

category: Epi curve: before vs after vaccination
stem: Two epidemic curves are drawn for the same disease in two towns. Town A's curve rises to a tall, sharp peak. Town B, where most residents were vaccinated beforehand, has a curve that stays low and flat. The flat curve in Town B is best explained by:

options.A: Town B having a much larger population than Town A
options.B: the disease being a different pathogen in Town B
options.C: Town B reporting its cases far less often than Town A
options.D: most of Town B being immune, so each case found fewer people to infect

stem: A city introduced a mask rule the same week its outbreak hit its peak. After that week, daily cases fell steadily. A news report credits the mask rule with ending the outbreak. The most scientifically careful response is to:

options.A: note that cases fall on their own after a peak, so the new rule's effect is unclear
options.B: agree with the news report, since the city's cases fell right after the new rule
options.C: agree with the news report, since mask rules reliably end almost every outbreak
options.D: decide, from the timing alone, that the mask rule must have made things much worse
